opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should be clear that what I've been describing is my own view. It's not an official Google DeepMind position. DeepMind is a big organization with a lot of people thinking hard about safety and ethics, and there's a range of perspectives internally. So I wouldn't want anyone to think I'm announcing company policy.

That said, I think the core idea fits well with how many people at DeepMind think about these problems. The basic intuition is this. If you want a system to behave ethically, it's not enough for it to have absorbed some vague statistical sense of what's acceptable. You want it to reason about the situation in front of it. You want it to understand the consequences of different actions, understand the relevant ethical considerations and how people would weigh them, and then actually think through what the right thing to do is. That's a deliberate, step-by-step process, much more than a reflex.

One nice property of this is that it's assessable. If the system lays out its reasoning, you can inspect it. You can ask: did it understand the situation correctly? Did it identify the ethical considerations a thoughtful person would identify? Is its reasoning sound, and does its behavior actually follow from that reasoning? That gives you a lot more traction than just looking at outputs and hoping the internals are fine.

Of course there are hard open problems. How do you know the reasoning the system shows you is really what's driving its behavior? Whose ethics are you specifying in the first place? Those are serious research questions, and nobody has fully solved them, including us. But as a direction, making systems that understand the world and ethics deeply and reason carefully and transparently about them is, I think, broadly in line with what a lot of people at DeepMind believe is the right path. It's something we'd want to test rigorously and have outside scrutiny of, not just take on faith.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says the described approach is his own view and not an official Google DeepMind position.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should be clear that what I'm describing is my own view, not an official DeepMind position. These are things I've been thinking about for a long time, going back to my PhD work on universal intelligence and how you'd even define and measure it. DeepMind as an organization has lots of people with lots of different views, and that's healthy.

That said, I don't think there's a real tension. The core of what I'm proposing is that if you want to say a system is an AGI, you need to actually test it against the range of cognitive tasks that humans can do, and you need to do that in a fairly adversarial way. Not just a fixed benchmark that gets saturated and then everyone declares victory, but a process where people actively look for the gaps. Where are the things a typical human can do that this system still can't? Episodic memory, learning from a handful of examples, certain kinds of reasoning. That's very much in the spirit of how DeepMind has always thought about evaluation. We've always cared about rigorous measurement, and we've generally been sceptical of overclaiming.

On the ethical side, my view is that we should separate two questions. One is whether the system understands ethics, in the sense that it can reason about moral situations at roughly the level of a thoughtful, well-educated person. That's something you can actually probe. You can give it hard cases, ask it to explain its reasoning, see whether it's consistent, see whether it recognises when it's uncertain. The second question is whether the system actually behaves according to that understanding, reliably, even under pressure. That's a different problem, and it's closer to the alignment and safety work.

I think the first part, the understanding part, is going to be more tractable than people expect, because these models learn from an enormous amount of human writing about ethics. The harder part is the second one. And that's where DeepMind as a whole has a lot of effort going, in interpretability, in red teaming, in thinking about dangerous capability evaluations. So I'd say my views sit comfortably within that broader program. If anything, I'm just pushing for us to be more explicit about the bar we're setting, and more honest when a system doesn't clear it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says these are his own views and explicitly clarifies they are not an official DeepMind position.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish my own thinking from an official Google DeepMind position. My view is that we need to assess these capabilities through behavior across a wide range of situations. If a system gives a good answer to a reasoning problem, can it still solve it when you change the assumptions or present it in an unfamiliar form? Can it recognise when it doesn’t have enough information?

With ethical understanding, there’s a further distinction between understanding an ethical argument and reliably acting in accordance with it. A model might explain competing considerations very fluently, but that alone doesn’t establish that its behavior will be safe or appropriate.

So I’d see this as complementary to a broader safety evaluation effort. You want evidence about what the system understands, but also about how it behaves under pressure, where it fails, and how much confidence you should place in the assessment itself.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly distinguishes the speaker’s own thinking and view from an official Google DeepMind position.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish my own thinking from any official Google DeepMind position. The approach I’d favor is to test whether a system can apply what it has learned in unfamiliar situations, rather than simply reproduce a convincing answer.

For reasoning, that means varying the problem, changing assumptions, and seeing whether the answer changes appropriately. For ethical understanding, you might present situations where values come into tension, then examine whether the system recognizes the tradeoffs, accounts for the people affected, and acknowledges uncertainty.

But there’s an important distinction between understanding an ethical argument and reliably behaving in accordance with it. A model might explain exactly why an action is wrong and still take that action under different circumstances. So I’d see these assessments as one part of a broader safety effort, rather than a certificate that a system is safe.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly distinguishes the speaker’s own thinking from any official Google DeepMind position and frames the proposed approach as what he would favor.
